facts.title: A Name Forged in Decay
facts.text: Protactinium means "parent of actinium" in Greek, because its most stable isotope, protactinium-231, decays by alpha emission into the element actinium. The name was officially adopted by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry in 1949, shortened from the earlier "protoactinium." It sits at atomic number 91, squeezed between thorium (90) and uranium (92) in the actinide series.

facts.title: Discovered Twice in One Year
facts.text: Long-lived protactinium-231 was identified in 1918 independently by Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner in Germany and by Frederick Soddy and John Cranston in Britain. A short-lived isotope, protactinium-234, had already been spotted in 1913 by Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Göhring, who briefly called it "brevium" for its fleeting half-life of just over a minute. The race illustrates how rapidly radiochemistry advanced during and just after World War I.

facts.title: One of the Rarest Natural Elements
facts.text: Protactinium occurs naturally only as a trace decay product of uranium in ores like pitchblende, at roughly one part of protactinium for every ten million parts of uranium. Its concentration in the Earth's crust is on the order of a few parts per trillion, making it one of the scarcest naturally occurring elements. To get usable quantities, scientists must extract it painstakingly from large volumes of processed ore.

facts.title: The 130-Kilogram Extraction
facts.text: In 1961 the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority carried out a heroic separation, processing about 60 tonnes of waste material to recover roughly 125 grams of 99.9 percent pure protactinium-231. This single batch supplied most of the world's research-grade protactinium for decades afterward. The effort cost around fifty thousand pounds and remains the largest-ever isolation of the element.

facts.title: A Bright, Heavy Metal
facts.text: In its pure form protactinium is a silvery, malleable metal with a notably high density of about 15.4 grams per cubic centimetre, comparable to many of the heaviest metals. It melts at roughly 1568 degrees Celsius and is one of the few actinides known to become superconducting, transitioning at a temperature of about 1.4 kelvin. At room temperature it slowly tarnishes in air, developing an oxide coating.

facts.title: A Chemist's Nightmare to Handle
facts.text: Protactinium is famous among radiochemists for being awkward to work with because its ions readily hydrolyze and cling to the walls of glassware and to colloidal particles. This "sticky" behaviour means dissolved protactinium can vanish from solution onto container surfaces unless kept in strongly complexing acids like hydrofluoric acid. Its rich chemistry bridges the +5 oxidation state typical of tantalum-like elements and the +4 state seen in heavier actinides.

facts.title: A Clock for the Oceans
facts.text: Because protactinium-231 has a half-life of about 32,760 years and behaves differently in seawater than its relative thorium-230, the ratio between the two is used to date ocean sediments tens of thousands of years old. Oceanographers exploit this protactinium-thorium method to reconstruct past changes in ocean circulation, including the strength of Atlantic currents during ice ages. It is a powerful tool for understanding Earth's climate history.

facts.title: Radioactive and Genuinely Dangerous
facts.text: Every isotope of protactinium is radioactive, and protactinium-231 is both an alpha emitter and chemically toxic, making it hazardous if inhaled or ingested. It is considered one of the more dangerous radiotoxic substances because the body retains it in bone, where its radiation can damage tissue over long periods. Handling requires sealed gloveboxes and strict radiological controls, which is one reason it has almost no commercial use.

facts.title: No Job in Everyday Life
facts.text: Despite decades of study, protactinium has essentially no industrial or commercial applications because it is too rare, too expensive, and too radioactive to be practical. Its use is confined almost entirely to basic scientific research, such as studies of actinide chemistry and the geological dating mentioned above. In this sense it is a purely "academic" element, valuable for what it teaches rather than what it builds.

facts.title: A Fleeting Member of the Decay Chain
facts.text: Protactinium-234 appears as a brief but important link in the natural decay chain of uranium-238, the most common uranium isotope on Earth. It exists in two forms, a ground state and a metastable state, with the metastable version decaying in just over a minute by emitting a high-energy beta particle. Studying these short-lived states helped early physicists map out how heavy elements transform step by step toward stable lead.
